title: Narcissus. Echo
titleEn: Narcissus and Echo, 1 of 2 — Metamorphoses III.339–436
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: A seer whose answers no one could fault is asked about a newborn boy, and says that he will live to old age only if he never comes to know himself. The child is Narcissus, born to the water-nymph Liriope, whom the river-god Cephisus trapped in his own current and raped. At sixteen Narcissus is wanted by young men and girls alike and lets none of them touch him; the nymph Echo, whom Juno has left able only to give back the last words she hears, falls in love with him, is refused, and wastes away in the woods until nothing of her is left but a voice. A scorned suitor prays that he may love and never have what he loves, Nemesis grants it, and Narcissus lies down at an untouched pool to drink and falls in love with the face in the water; the part breaks off with Ovid speaking to him directly.

advisory.lede: The river-god Cephisus traps the nymph Liriope in his own current and rapes her; Narcissus is the child of that rape.
advisory.more: It occupies parts of three lines (III.342-344). Ovid gives the assault no more room than the phrase vim tulit, 'he brought force to bear' - the ordinary Latin for rape - and goes straight on to the birth. Lectorium translates the phrase as what it says and presents the passage unaltered.

sentences.t:
Ille per Aonias fama celeberrimus urbes
inreprehensa dabat populo responsa petenti.
sentences.l: He, most celebrated by report throughout the Aonian cities, was giving unfaultable answers to the people that asked.
sentences.i: His fame ran through the cities of Aonia, and he gave the people who came asking answers no one could fault.
sentences.n: 'He' is the prophet the tale turns on, called fatidicus vates, 'the fate-speaking seer', at line 348; the pronoun points back beyond the opening of this part, and no name for him is printed in these lines. Aonia is a name for Boeotia, the country round Thebes, so 'the Aonian cities' is simply the towns of that region. inreprehensa is Magnus's spelling of irreprehensa, 'not to be caught out'; petenti is a participle agreeing with populo, the people doing the asking. dabat is imperfect: this went on and on.

sentences.t:
Prima fide vocisque ratae temptamina sumpsit
caerula Liriope.
sentences.l: The first trials of his trustworthiness and of his ratified voice sea-blue Liriope took up.
sentences.i: The first test of whether he could be trusted, of whether his voice came true, was made by sea-blue Liriope.
sentences.n: fide is the old genitive of fides, 'trust', standing parallel to vocis ratae, 'of the voice ratified' - ratus is the participle of reor used of what the event confirms. temptamina are 'trials, test cases'. The subject is held to the very end of the sentence, so the reader has the test before he has the tester; the literal keeps that order. caerula, 'dark sea-blue', is the colour-word of water and marks Liriope as a water-nymph before anything else is said of her.

sentences.t:
Quam quondam flumine curvo
implicuit clausaeque suis Cephisus in undis
vim tulit.
sentences.l: And her once with his curving stream Cephisus wrapped round, and to her, shut in in his own waves, he brought force.
sentences.i: Cephisus had once wound his curving current about her, closed her inside his own water, and raped her.
sentences.n: A connecting relative: Quam at the head of a sentence is 'and her', not a question - Latin joins sentences with a relative where English begins a new one. Cephisus is the Boeotian river, a god as much as a water, which is why he can take her by folding his own stream round her. clausae is dative, agreeing with her, and goes with the phrase vim tulit: vim ferre, like vim inferre, is the standard Latin for rape, and that is what the line reports.

sentences.t:
Enixa est utero pulcherrima pleno
infantem, nymphis iam tunc qui posset amari,
Narcissumque vocat.
sentences.l: She brought forth from her full womb, most beautiful, a child who even then could be loved by nymphs, and calls him Narcissus.
sentences.i: Her womb full, that loveliest of nymphs bore a boy who even then was one nymphs could fall in love with - and she names him Narcissus.
sentences.n: enixa est is deponent, passive in form and active in sense: she is the one giving birth. utero pleno is ablative, 'with womb full', the ordinary way of saying she carried to term. qui posset amari is a relative clause of characteristic in the subjunctive, 'the sort of boy who could be loved' - his beauty is put as a capacity, not an event - and nymphis is the dative of agent that a passive infinitive takes in verse. Then vocat swings into the present after the perfect enixa est, the historic present pulling the naming close. Magnus prints nymphis, 'by nymphs'; some editions print nymphe.

sentences.t:
De quo consultus, an esset
tempora maturae visurus longa senectae,
fatidicus vates “si se non noverit” inquit.
sentences.l: Consulted about him, whether he would be going to see the long span of ripe old age, the fate-speaking seer says, 'if he will not have known himself.'
sentences.i: Asked about the child - would he live to see the long years of a ripe old age? - the prophet answered: 'If he never knows himself.'
sentences.n: an esset ... visurus is an indirect question in the subjunctive using the future participle, the Latin way of putting a future inside a reported question. The answer is a condition with no main clause attached: si se non noverit is future perfect, 'if he shall not have known himself', and the 'yes, he will' is left for the questioner to supply. The perfect of nosco means 'know' outright, not 'get to know', so the force of the future perfect is simply 'if he does not know himself'. The seer's condition inverts the Delphic instruction to know yourself: here self-knowledge is the thing that kills.

sentences.t:
Vana diu visa est vox auguris: exitus illam
resque probat letique genus novitasque furoris.
sentences.l: Empty for a long time the augur's utterance seemed: the outcome and the event prove it, and the kind of death and the strangeness of the madness.
sentences.i: For a long while the seer's word looked like nothing: the outcome proved it - the event, the manner of his death, the strangeness of his madness.
sentences.n: illam is the vox of the line before, the thing that gets proved. probat is singular with four subjects piled behind it - Latin lets the verb agree with the nearest and the list accumulate after. augur is strictly a diviner by birds, used loosely here of any prophet. leti genus and novitas furoris tell the reader in advance how it ends without telling him what happens, and novitas is 'newness, strangeness' - a kind of madness not seen before.

sentences.t:
Namque ter ad quinos unum Cephisius annum
addiderat poteratque puer iuvenisque videri:
multi illum iuvenes, multae cupiere puellae.
sentences.l: For to thrice five the son of Cephisus had added one year, and he could seem a boy and a young man: many young men, many girls desired him.
sentences.i: For the son of Cephisus had added a single year to three times five, and could pass for boy or man alike: many youths desired him, and many girls.
sentences.n: ter ad quinos unum annum is sixteen said the long way round, as verse counts. Cephisius is a patronymic, 'son of Cephisus', from the river of line 343. poterat ... videri, 'could be seen, could seem', is the point: at that age he answers to both descriptions at once. cupiere is the poetic third-person plural perfect, the short form of cupiverunt - the ending -ere for -erunt is standard in verse, and you should read it as a plain perfect. The desire runs both ways, iuvenes and puellae, and Ovid states it flatly.

sentences.t:
Sed fuit in tenera tam dura superbia forma:
nulli illum iuvenes, nullae tetigere puellae.
sentences.l: But there was in that soft beauty so hard a pride: no young men, no girls touched him.
sentences.i: But in that tender beauty there sat so hard a pride: no youth, no girl ever touched him.
sentences.n: The line works by setting tenera against dura, soft shape against hard pride, in the same phrase. And 355 rebuilds 353 with the quantities emptied out: multi ... multae becomes nulli ... nullae, and the verb changes from desiring to touching - the same frame with nobody left in it. tetigere is again the -ere perfect, here from tango; 'touched' keeps its whole range, from laying a hand on him to moving him at all.

sentences.t:
Adspicit hunc trepidos agitantem in retia cervos
vocalis nymphe, quae nec reticere loquenti,
nec prior ipsa loqui didicit, resonabilis Echo.
sentences.l: Him, driving frightened deer into the nets, the voiceful nymph catches sight of - she who learned neither to keep silent towards one speaking, nor herself to speak first - resounding Echo.
sentences.i: The nymph of the voice caught sight of him as he drove terrified deer into the nets - she who never learned to hold her tongue when another spoke, nor to speak first herself: Echo, who gives back sound.
sentences.n: Adspicit is Magnus's spelling of aspicit, and it is a historic present: the meeting is put in front of us as it happens. The subject is withheld through two whole lines and lands last of all in her own name, with vocalis nymphe at one end and resonabilis Echo at the other, wrapped round the two things she cannot do. didicit governs both infinitives; loquenti is the dative that reticere takes, 'be silent towards someone who is speaking'. Her condition is stated as two failures to learn: she cannot keep quiet when addressed, and she cannot begin.

sentences.t:
Corpus adhuc Echo, non vox erat; et tamen usum
garrula non alium, quam nunc habet, oris habebat,
reddere de multis ut verba novissima posset.
sentences.l: Echo was still a body, not a voice; and yet, chatterbox that she was, she had no other use of her mouth than she has now: to be able to give back, out of many, the last words.
sentences.i: Echo was still a body then, not a voice - and yet, for all her chattering, her mouth could already do no more than it does now: give back, out of many words, only the last.
sentences.n: adhuc, 'still', and nunc, 'now', set the story's time against the reader's: at this point in the tale she has a body, and the voice-only Echo is what she has since become. usum ... oris, 'the use of her mouth', is the general term, and the ut-clause spells out exactly what that use amounts to, with its verb in the subjunctive (posset). garrula, 'talkative', is nominative and describes her, not the mouth. de multis is 'out of many [words]', the noun supplied from verba; novissima is the superlative of novus in its normal Latin sense of 'last, latest', not 'newest'.

sentences.t:
Fecerat hoc Iuno, quia, cum deprendere posset
cum Iove saepe suo nymphas in monte iacentes,
illa deam longo prudens sermone tenebat,
dum fugerent nymphae.
sentences.l: Juno had done this, because, when she was often able to catch nymphs lying with her own Jupiter on the mountain, that one knowingly held the goddess with long talk, until the nymphs might escape.
sentences.i: Juno had made her so, because, whenever she might have caught the nymphs lying with her own Jupiter on the mountain, Echo knew exactly what she was doing and held the goddess in long conversation until they could get away.
sentences.n: The pluperfect fecerat steps back a stage to explain the disability just described. cum ... posset is circumstantial with the subjunctive, 'when she was in a position to catch them'; suo is pointed, since Jupiter is Juno's own husband and the nymphs are lying with him. prudens is a nominative adjective doing adverbial work, 'knowing what she was about'. dum fugerent takes the subjunctive because the delay is purposeful - she talks so that they may get clear, not merely while they do. illa is Echo, deam is Juno. Magnus prints cum Iove, 'with Jupiter'; some editions print sub Iove, 'under Jupiter'.

sentences.t:
Postquam Saturnia sensit
“huius” ait “linguae, qua sum delusa, potestas
parva tibi dabitur vocisque brevissimus usus”:
reque minas firmat.
sentences.l: After the daughter of Saturn perceived it, 'of this tongue,' she says, 'by which I have been tricked, small power will be given to you, and the very briefest use of your voice': and by the event she makes her threats good.
sentences.i: When Saturn's daughter saw through it: 'This tongue that fooled me,' she said, 'you shall have only the smallest power of it - the briefest possible use of your voice.' And she made the threat good in fact.
sentences.n: Saturnia, 'daughter of Saturn', is Juno named by descent. huius ... linguae is genitive depending on potestas, and Ovid splits the phrase across the interrupting ait so that the tongue is the first word out of her mouth. qua sum delusa is the ablative of the thing she was tricked by. re in reque minas firmat is the ablative of res, 'by the fact, by the event': the threat is not only spoken but carried out. The punishment is cut to fit - the instrument of the offence is the faculty curtailed.

sentences.t:
Tamen haec in fine loquendi
ingeminat voces auditaque verba reportat.
sentences.l: Still, she at the end of speaking doubles voices and carries back the words she has heard.
sentences.i: Even so, at the end of what is said she redoubles the sounds and brings back the words she has heard.
sentences.n: haec is Echo, 'this one'. in fine loquendi uses the gerund in the genitive, 'at the end of the speaking', and the phrase is precise about her limit: only the tail of a sentence comes back. ingeminat is 'doubles' - the sound repeated, not answered. auditaque verba is the perfect participle of audio agreeing with verba, 'the heard words', which English has to open out into a clause. Magnus prints Tamen, 'still, even so'; some editions print tantum, 'only'.

sentences.t:
Ergo ubi Narcissum per devia rura vagantem
vidit et incaluit, sequitur vestigia furtim,
quoque magis sequitur, flamma propiore calescit,
sentences.l: And so, when she saw Narcissus wandering through the pathless country and grew hot, she follows his tracks stealthily, and by how much the more she follows, by so much she warms with a nearer flame,
sentences.i: So when she saw Narcissus roaming the trackless countryside and caught fire, she followed his footsteps in secret - and the more she followed, the nearer the flame and the hotter she grew.
sentences.n: quoque here is not the adverb 'also': it is quo-que, the ablative of degree of difference, 'and by which the more', opening the Latin 'the more ..., the more ...' pattern with the answering eo left to be understood. This trap is worth remembering: quoque is as often quo-que, two words, as it is the adverb 'also'. incaluit is the inceptive of caleo, 'grew warm', and the heat it starts runs straight on into the flame. The tenses shift from perfect (vidit, incaluit) to present (sequitur, calescit) inside the one sentence, the historic present taking over as the pursuit begins.

sentences.t:
non aliter, quam cum summis circumlita taedis
admotas rapiunt vivacia sulphura flammas.
sentences.l: not otherwise than when the living sulphur smeared round the tips of torches snatches at the flames brought near.
sentences.i: just as the quick sulphur daubed on the heads of torches snatches at a flame held close to it.
sentences.n: non aliter quam, 'not otherwise than', is the standard way Ovid opens a simile. The picture is a torch made ready for lighting: sulphur, brimstone, was smeared on the head (summis ... taedis, 'at the tops of the torches') because it takes fire instantly. circumlita is the perfect participle agreeing with sulphura, 'smeared round'; admotas flammas, 'the flames brought up', is the object not of that participle but of rapiunt. vivacia is 'full of life, quick to live', of a substance that catches at once, and rapiunt is violent - the sulphur does not wait to be lit, it seizes. The comparison is to Echo catching fire, not to Narcissus.

sentences.t:
O quotiens voluit blandis accedere dictis
et molles adhibere preces: natura repugnat
nec sinit incipiat.
sentences.l: Oh, how often she wanted to approach with coaxing words and to bring soft entreaties to bear! Her nature fights back and does not allow that she begin.
sentences.i: How often she longed to approach him with soft words, to put a gentle plea to him! Her nature fought her and would not let her start.
sentences.n: O quotiens is exclamation, not question - the poet breaking in on his own narrative. blandis ... dictis is ablative, the means of the approach. natura here is her condition, the thing Juno left her with, not the natural world. sinit incipiat is a subjunctive without ut, common in verse: 'allows [that] she begin'. Everything the sentence is about is compressed into that one verb - what she cannot do is not speak but speak first. The tenses drop from perfect voluit to present repugnat and sinit, the standing rule of her state.

sentences.t:
Sed, quod sinit, illa parata est
exspectare sonos, ad quos sua verba remittat.
sentences.l: But - the thing it does allow - she is ready to wait for sounds, to which she may send back her own words.
sentences.i: But what it does allow, she is ready for: to wait for sounds she can send her own words back to.
sentences.n: quod sinit stands outside the frame of the sentence, 'as to what it does allow'; the subject of sinit is still natura from the line before. ad quos ... remittat is a relative clause of purpose with the subjunctive, 'sounds to which she may send back' - she waits with an end in view. sua verba, 'her own words', is the joke stated straight: they are hers only in that she is the one returning them.

sentences.t:
Forte puer comitum seductus ab agmine fido,
dixerat “ecquis adest?” et “adest!” responderat Echo.
sentences.l: By chance the boy, drawn apart from the trusty band of his companions, had said, 'is anyone here?' and 'here!' Echo had answered.
sentences.i: As it happened the boy had strayed from the faithful band of his companions: he called out, 'Is anyone here?' - and 'Here!' Echo answered.
sentences.n: The echo works in English for free: adest is the last word of his question and a complete answer on its own. The pluperfects (dixerat, responderat) set the exchange a moment behind the narrative, so we arrive just after it has begun. seductus is the perfect participle of seduco, 'led apart', and ab agmine fido is the ablative of separation - he is away from his hunting party, which is why there is nobody there.

sentences.t:
Hic stupet, utque aciem partes dimittit in omnes,
voce “veni!” magna clamat: vocat illa vocantem.
sentences.l: He is astonished, and as he sends his gaze off into all quarters, with a great voice he shouts 'come!': she calls the one calling.
sentences.i: He stands amazed, and as he casts his eyes in every direction, he shouts at the top of his voice, 'Come!' - and she calls back to the caller.
sentences.n: Ovid does not quote her here; he describes the echo in the grammar instead - vocat illa vocantem, the same verb turned back on itself, active participle answered by active verb. aciem is the eye's sharpness and so 'the gaze'; dimittit ... in partes omnes is 'sends it off into every quarter'. voce ... magna is ablative and is split round the quoted word, so that the shout stands inside its own loudness.

sentences.t:
Respicit et rursus nullo veniente “quid” inquit
“me fugis?” et totidem, quot dixit, verba recepit.
sentences.l: He looks back, and again, with no one coming, he says, 'why do you flee me?' - and he received back as many words as he spoke.
sentences.i: He looked round; still no one came. 'Why do you run from me?' he says - and got back exactly as many words as he had spoken.
sentences.n: Ovid does not quote Echo's reply here. totidem, quot dixit, verba - the same number of words - leaves the reader to work out that me fugis, cut loose from quid, answers the question all by itself. nullo veniente is an ablative absolute, 'with no one coming'; totidem ... quot is the correlative pair, 'just as many ... as'.

sentences.t:
Perstat et, alternae deceptus imagine vocis,
“huc coeamus!” ait: nullique libentius umquam
responsura sono “coeamus” rettulit Echo,
sentences.l: He persists and, deceived by the likeness of the alternating voice, 'let us come together here!' he says: and never was Echo going to answer any sound more gladly - 'let us come together,' she gave back.
sentences.i: He keeps at it and, taken in by the image of a voice answering turn about, 'Come here, let's get together!' he says. Echo never answered any sound more gladly in her life: 'Let's get together.'
sentences.n: alternae ... vocis is 'of the voice that comes turn about', and imagine is the ablative of means with deceptus - it is the semblance of an answering voice that takes him in. Then the pun the scene turns on: coeo means plainly 'come together, meet' - and also 'couple, have intercourse'. Narcissus means the first; Echo, returning the identical word, means the second, and Ovid says outright that she never answered anything more gladly. English 'get together' carries both senses the way coeamus does, so the idiomatic reproduces the joke while the literal keeps the transparent sense visible. responsura is a future participle - she is about to answer, eager before she speaks.

sentences.t:
et verbis favet ipsa suis egressaque silva
ibat, ut iniceret sperato bracchia collo.
sentences.l: and she herself is favourable to her own words, and having gone out from the wood she was going, so that she might throw her arms round the hoped-for neck.
sentences.i: and she backs her own words: out of the wood she came, going to throw her arms about the neck she had hoped for.
sentences.n: faveo takes the dative, so verbis ... suis is 'to her own words' - she acts on what she has just said, because the borrowed words happened to say what she wanted. egressa is the perfect participle of the deponent egredior, active in sense, with silva a bare ablative of separation. ut iniceret is a purpose clause in the imperfect subjunctive after the imperfect ibat, so the throwing never happens - she was on her way to it. sperato ... collo is the dative iniceret governs, and the epithet is startling: the neck itself is 'hoped-for'.

sentences.t:
Ille fugit fugiensque “manus complexibus aufer:
ante” ait “emoriar, quam sit tibi copia nostri.”
sentences.l: He flees, and as he flees, 'take your hands away from embraces: I will die first,' he says, 'before there is to you the enjoyment of us.'
sentences.i: He runs, and running: 'Hands off - get away from me! I'd sooner die than let you have me.'
sentences.n: fugiens is the present participle of fugio picked up straight from fugit, 'he flees and fleeing', so the motion never stops. manus ... aufer is the imperative of aufero with the ablative complexibus, 'take your hands away from embraces'. ante ... quam is the pair 'sooner ... than', split across the interrupting ait; emoriar is the future of the deponent emorior, 'I shall die outright', and sit is the subjunctive the quam-clause requires. copia is 'plenty, abundance' and so 'access, the having of'; nostri is the objective genitive of nos standing for mei. The English is built so that its tail can stand alone, because in the next line it will have to.

sentences.t: Rettulit illa nihil nisi “sit tibi copia nostri.”
sentences.l: She gave back nothing except 'may there be to you the enjoyment of us.'
sentences.i: She gave back nothing but: 'let you have me.'
sentences.n: Here the echo inverts the sentence by amputating it. ante emoriar quam sit tibi copia nostri is 'I shall die before you have the enjoyment of me'; cut loose from ante ... quam, the same words become a wish - 'may you have the enjoyment of me.' The subjunctive sit, which the quam-clause had governed, is left with nothing over it and reads as a wish instead. The English is built so its tail turns exactly as the Latin's does.

sentences.t:
Spreta latet silvis pudibundaque frondibus ora
protegit et solis ex illo vivit in antris.
Sed tamen haeret amor crescitque dolore repulsae.
sentences.l: Spurned, she hides in the woods and covers her shamed face with leaves, and from that time lives in lonely caves. But still her love clings, and grows with the pain of the rejection.
sentences.i: Rejected, she took cover in the woods, hid her face in the leaves for shame, and from that day lived in caves, alone. Yet the love holds on, and grows with the pain of being refused.
sentences.n: spreta is the perfect participle of sperno, nominative, agreeing with her: 'having been spurned'. ora is the poetic plural for a single face, and pudibunda, 'full of shame', is the neuter plural adjective agreeing with it. ex illo is 'from that [time]', with tempore left out. solis ... in antris is 'in caves that are alone' - the word for solitude put on the caves and meant of her. dolore repulsae is ablative of cause, and repulsa is the noun for a rebuff.

sentences.t:
Extenuant vigiles corpus miserabile curae,
adducitque cutem macies et in aera sucus
corporis omnis abit.
sentences.l: Wakeful cares thin down her pitiable body, and leanness draws her skin tight, and all the moisture of her body goes off into the air.
sentences.i: Sleepless cares wear her wretched body away; the thinness pulls her skin tight, and all the sap of her body goes off into the air.
sentences.n: vigiles curae are 'wakeful cares', cares that keep her awake - the adjective belongs to her and is handed to them. adducit cutem is the physical verb: the skin is drawn in and tightened over nothing. sucus is the juice or sap of a body, its moisture, and omnis agrees with sucus, not with corporis. in aera keeps the Greek accusative of the Greek noun aer. This is the first stage of the change: the wet part of her leaves first.

sentences.t:
Vox tantum atque ossa supersunt:
vox manet; ossa ferunt lapidis traxisse figuram.
sentences.l: Only voice and bones are left over: the voice remains; the bones, they say, drew on the form of stone.
sentences.i: Only voice and bones are left: the voice stays; the bones, they say, took on the shape of stone.
sentences.n: ferunt is 'they say, the story goes' - third person plural with no expressed subject - and it introduces the accusative and infinitive ossa ... traxisse, with ossa as the subject of the infinitive. Ovid is marking the stone as report rather than his own assertion. traxisse figuram, 'to have drawn on a shape', is ordinary Latin for taking on a form. The two things that survive are the two that could: the sound she had been reduced to, and the frame that outlasts flesh.

sentences.t:
inde latet silvis nulloque in monte videtur;
omnibus auditur: sonus est, qui vivit in illa.
sentences.l: From then on she lies hidden in the woods and is seen on no mountain; by all she is heard: it is sound that lives in her.
sentences.i: From then on she lies hidden in the forests and is seen on no hillside; everyone hears her: what lives on in her is sound.
sentences.n: The two passive verbs are the whole of what she now is - videtur, 'she is seen', denied, and auditur, 'she is heard', granted, with omnibus the dative of agent that verse allows, 'by everybody'. silvis is a plain ablative of place without a preposition, as poetry regularly writes it. In the last clause sonus is put first for weight: it is not she who lives on, but the sound.

sentences.t:
Sic hanc, sic alias undis aut montibus ortas
luserat hic nymphas, sic coetus ante viriles.
sentences.l: So this one, so other nymphs risen from the waters or the mountains he had mocked, so before that the gatherings of men.
sentences.i: So he had made a fool of her, and of other nymphs born of the water or the hills, and before them of the companies of men.
sentences.n: Three sics, one for each group he has used the same way; hanc is Echo, and nymphas is held back into the second line so that the whole catalogue arrives before the noun it belongs to. ortas is the perfect participle of the deponent orior with the ablative of origin, 'sprung from waters or mountains'. ludo here is 'make sport of, trick', not 'play'. coetus viriles, 'companies of males', answers the multi ... iuvenes of line 353: the young men wanted him too, and were treated the same.

sentences.t:
Inde manus aliquis despectus ad aethera tollens
“sic amet ipse licet sic non potiatur amato!”
dixerat. Adsensit precibus Rhamnusia iustis.
sentences.l: Then someone, looked down on, raising his hands to the upper air, had said, 'so may he himself love, granted that so he may not gain possession of what he loves!' The Rhamnusian goddess assented to those just prayers.
sentences.i: Then someone he had scorned lifted his hands to heaven: 'So let him love, and so let him never have what he loves!' The goddess of Rhamnus assented - the prayer was just.
sentences.n: despectus is the perfect participle of despicio agreeing with aliquis, 'one who had been looked down on'. licet takes the subjunctive and is concessive here, 'granted that, even though': the wish is not that he love, but that the loving get him nothing, and licet is what turns a wish into a curse. potior is deponent and takes the ablative, so amato is 'the one loved'. ipse is nominative and emphasises the subject - 'may he himself love' - and the curse asks nothing about who the beloved will be; that it turns out to be himself is the story's own answer. Rhamnusia is Nemesis, named from her cult at Rhamnus in Attica: the goddess who evens out what is undeserved.

sentences.t:
Fons erat inlimis, nitidis argenteus undis,
quem neque pastores neque pastae monte capellae
contigerant aliudve pecus,
sentences.l: There was a spring, unmuddied, silvery with its shining waters, which neither shepherds nor she-goats pastured on the mountain had touched, nor any other flock,
sentences.i: There was a pool without silt, silver with its bright water, that no shepherd had ever touched, nor she-goats grazing the mountain, nor any other beast,
sentences.n: Fons erat is the standard opening of an ecphrasis, the set-piece description of a place; here it is what the boy is about to walk into. inlimis is Magnus's spelling of illimis, 'without mud', a negative built on limus, silt. argenteus, 'of silver', is used of the look of the water, with nitidis ... undis as the ablative that specifies it. pastae is the perfect participle of the deponent pascor, 'having grazed', with monte a bare ablative of place. The whole description proceeds by subtraction: everything that might have disturbed the water is named and denied.

sentences.t:
quem nulla volucris
nec fera turbarat nec lapsus ab arbore ramus.
sentences.l: which no bird nor wild beast had troubled, nor a branch fallen from a tree.
sentences.i: which no bird had troubled, nor wild animal, nor a branch dropping from a tree.
sentences.n: turbarat is the syncopated pluperfect for turbaverat: Latin regularly drops the -ve- of perfect stems, and verse prefers the shorter form. lapsus is the perfect participle of the deponent labor, 'having slipped, fallen', active in sense. The relative quem is repeated from the line before for a second run at the same pool, and the list ends on the smallest disturbance imaginable, a twig, to say that not even that had happened.

sentences.t:
Gramen erat circa, quod proximus umor alebat,
silvaque sole locum passura tepescere nullo.
sentences.l: There was grass around, which the moisture close by fed, and a wood going to allow the place to grow warm by no sun.
sentences.i: Grass grew round it, fed by the water at its edge, and a wood that would let no sun warm the place.
sentences.n: passura is the future participle of the deponent patior agreeing with silva, 'about to allow, such as would allow', and it governs the accusative and infinitive locum ... tepescere. sole ... nullo is the ablative of means, pushed to the two ends of the line so that the negative lands last of all. tepescere is inceptive: 'to begin to be warm' - not heat, only the loss of coolness, which is exactly what the wood prevents.

sentences.t:
Hic puer, et studio venandi lassus et aestu,
procubuit faciemque loci fontemque secutus.
dumque sitim sedare cupit, sitis altera crevit.
sentences.l: Here the boy, tired both by his zeal for hunting and by the heat, lay down, having followed the look of the place and the spring. And while he desires to settle one thirst, another thirst grew.
sentences.i: Here the boy lay down, worn out by the heat and by his passion for the hunt, drawn on by the look of the place and by the water. And while he wants to quench one thirst, a second thirst grew in him.
sentences.n: studio venandi has the gerund in the genitive, 'of hunting', and the two ablatives joined by et ... et are the two things that tire him, his own eagerness and the weather. secutus is the perfect participle of the deponent sequor and is active in sense, 'having followed' - he came here after the look of the place, not the other way about. sitim sedare is the plain Latin for quenching a thirst, 'to settle' it; sitis altera is the second thirst the sight of the water will start. The tense moves from present cupit to perfect crevit, so the new thirst is already in place before the old one is dealt with.

sentences.t:
Dumque bibit, visae correptus imagine formae
spem sine corpore amat: corpus putat esse, quod unda est
sentences.l: And while he drinks, seized by the image of the beauty he has seen, he loves a hope without a body: he thinks that to be a body which is water.
sentences.i: And as he drinks, caught by the image of the beauty he sees, he falls in love with a hope that has no body: he takes for a body what is water.
sentences.n: correptus is the perfect participle of corripio, passive - 'snatched up' by the image, which stands in the ablative. visae ... formae is the genitive with imagine, 'the image of the shape he has seen'. spem sine corpore amat puts the whole error in four words: the thing he loves has no body, only the hope of one. corpus putat esse, quod unda est is accusative and infinitive after putat. Magnus prints unda, 'water'; some editions print umbra, 'a shadow' - and Magnus's is the harder mistake, since it is not a shadow he takes for a body but water itself.

sentences.t:
adstupet ipse sibi, vultuque inmotus eodem
haeret, ut e Pario formatum marmore signum.
sentences.l: He himself stands amazed at himself, and unmoving with the same expression he sticks fast, like a statue shaped out of Parian marble.
sentences.i: He gazes at himself in astonishment, and stays fixed there, his face never changing, like a figure carved from Parian marble.
sentences.n: adstupet is Magnus's spelling of astupet, a rare compound meaning 'be stunned at', and it takes the dative sibi - the reflexive is the point, since the thing that stuns him is himself. inmotus, 'unmoved', is nominative and describes him, with the ablative vultu ... eodem, 'with that same face', wrapped round it. formatum is the perfect participle of formo agreeing with signum. Paros in the Cyclades supplied the white marble Greek and Roman sculptors prized; the comparison makes him into the same kind of thing he is looking at, an image with no life in it.

sentences.t:
Spectat humi positus geminum, sua lumina, sidus
et dignos Baccho, dignos et Apolline crines
impubesque genas et eburnea colla decusque
oris et in niveo mixtum candore ruborem,
sentences.l: Laid on the ground he gazes at the twin star that is his own eyes, and at his hair worthy of Bacchus, worthy of Apollo too, and his beardless cheeks and ivory neck and the grace of his mouth and the redness mixed into a snowy whiteness,
sentences.i: Stretched on the ground he gazes at the twin stars that are his own eyes, at hair fit for Bacchus, fit for Apollo, at his smooth cheeks, his ivory throat, the beauty of his mouth, and the flush mixed into snow-white skin,
sentences.n: humi is a locative, 'on the ground'. sua lumina sits in apposition inside the phrase geminum ... sidus, 'the twin star' - the two eyes are one constellation, and Latin can plant the gloss in the middle of the phrase where English needs a dash. dignus takes the ablative, hence Baccho and Apolline: both gods are pictured as young men with long unshorn hair. colla is the poetic plural for one neck, the same idiom used of Echo's face at line 393. mixtum agrees with ruborem, and in niveo ... candore is where the red is mixed. The catalogue is the standard inventory of a beautiful body, strung on a single chain of et - except that the body being inventoried is the looker's own.

sentences.t: cunctaque miratur, quibus est mirabilis ipse.
sentences.l: and he marvels at all the things by which he himself is marvellous.
sentences.i: and he wonders at everything that makes him a wonder.
sentences.n: One root used twice, miratur and mirabilis: he does the admiring and he is the thing admired. miror is deponent, active in sense, and takes cuncta as its object; quibus is the ablative of cause with mirabilis, 'the things on account of which he is worth wondering at'. The whole predicament of the tale is folded into a single verse.

sentences.t:
Se cupit imprudens et qui probat, ipse probatur,
dumque petit, petitur, pariterque accendit et ardet.
sentences.l: He desires himself, not knowing it, and the one who approves is himself approved, and while he seeks he is sought, and equally he kindles and burns.
sentences.i: Without knowing it he desires himself; the one who admires is the one admired; while he pursues, he is pursued; he lights the fire and burns in it.
sentences.n: Two pairs set an active verb against its own passive at once - probat and probatur, petit and petitur - so that the grammar performs the reflexiveness the story is about. The third pair works differently: ardet is not the passive of accendit but an active intransitive, 'he is on fire', so he lights the blaze in the same breath in which he burns in it. imprudens is prudens with its negative prefix, the same word used of Echo at line 364 when she knew exactly what she was doing; here it is reversed. probo is 'approve, find good', not 'prove'. pariter, 'in equal measure', holds the last pair level.

sentences.t:
Inrita fallaci quotiens dedit oscula fonti!
In mediis quotiens visum captantia collum
bracchia mersit aquis, nec se deprendit in illis!
sentences.l: How often he gave useless kisses to the deceiving spring! How often he plunged in the middle waters arms that kept trying to catch the neck he saw, and did not catch himself in them!
sentences.i: How often he pressed kisses that came to nothing on the lying water! How often he sank his arms in mid-pool, reaching for the neck he could see, and never caught hold of himself there!
sentences.n: quotiens twice, in exclamation and not question, matching the O quotiens used of Echo's longing at line 375. inrita is Magnus's spelling of irrita, 'not ratified, taking no effect' - a legal word for something that fails. fallaci ... fonti is the dative with dedit oscula. captantia is the present participle of the frequentative capto, 'keep trying to seize', agreeing with bracchia, with visum ... collum as its object; in mediis ... aquis is ablative with in, 'in mid-water', and Ovid stretches it across the whole sentence. deprendit is the verb used of Juno's chance to catch the nymphs at line 362 - here the one thing he cannot catch is himself.

sentences.t:
Quid videat, nescit: sed quod videt, uritur illo,
atque oculos idem, qui decipit, incitat error.
sentences.l: What he is seeing, he does not know: but by what he does see, he is set on fire, and the same mistake that deceives his eyes excites them.
sentences.i: What he is looking at, he does not know: but what he does see sets him alight, and the same error that fools his eyes goads them on.
sentences.n: The two halves are deliberately matched and differ in mood: quid videat is an indirect question and takes the subjunctive, quod videt is a plain relative with the indicative. He does not know what the thing is, but the thing he does see is real enough to burn him. illo is the ablative of cause with uritur, which is passive, 'he is burned by it'. In the second line error, the mistake itself, is made the agent, and it does two opposite things to the same pair of eyes: deceives them and drives them on.

sentences.t:
Credule, quid frusta simulacra fugacia captas?
quod petis, est nusquam; quod amas, avertere, perdes.
sentences.l: Credulous one, why do you try in vain to catch fleeting likenesses? What you seek is nowhere; what you love - turn away, and you will lose it.
sentences.i: You credulous boy, why keep snatching to no purpose at images that slip away? What you are after is nowhere at all; what you love, turn away and you destroy.
sentences.n: Ovid breaks off the narrative to address Narcissus directly - apostrophe, with the vocative Credule and second-person verbs. captas is the frequentative again, the same verb as the captantia bracchia of line 428, 'keep trying to catch'. avertere is the second-singular imperative of the middle-passive, 'turn yourself away', not the passive infinitive, and perdes is future indicative, so the two clauses work as a condition with no 'if': turn away, and you lose it. Magnus prints frusta, which as a word is the plural of frustum, 'a scrap'; the sense requires frustra, 'in vain', which some editions print. Lectorium prints its witness unaltered.

sentences.t: Ista repercussae, quam cernis, imaginis umbra est:
sentences.l: That thing, which you make out, is the shadow of an image thrown back:
sentences.i: What you are looking at is the shadow of a reflection:
sentences.n: repercussae ... imaginis is genitive, 'of an image struck back': repercutio is the physical verb for light or sound rebounding, the same idea that made Echo what she is. The relative clause quam cernis is slipped inside that genitive phrase, and the feminine quam picks up ista ... umbra, 'that shadow which you see'. umbra is 'shadow' and so 'a thing with nothing in it' - the weakest word available for what he loves.

sentences.t:
nil habet ista sui; tecum venitque manetque,
tecum discedet, si tu discedere possis.
sentences.l: That thing has nothing of its own; with you it comes and stays, with you it will go away, if you should be able to go away.
sentences.i: It has nothing of its own; it comes with you and stays with you, and with you it will leave - if you could ever leave.
sentences.n: sui is the genitive of the reflexive, partitive with nil: 'nothing of itself, nothing that is its own'. The verbs run through the tenses - present venit and manet, future discedet - and the -que ... -que pairing is the poetic double link that English can only render with 'and ... and'. The last clause is a condition with the subjunctive possis, the doubtful kind: not 'when you leave' but 'if you could' - and the doubt is where the sting is.
